_about: The Capelli Institute catalog. ONE source of truth for every book, edition, and lecture. Pages are generated from this file (tools/build-pages.py) and assets/data/catalog.js is derived from it for the in-page edition selector. Add a title here, run the generator, and the site has a product page. Commerce fields (price, sku, isbn, buyUrl, stock) are structured so a checkout can be attached later without a redesign. All copy below is transcribed from Sam Capelli's own cover art and sheets; nothing is invented. Fields set to null are awaiting the client.

lectures.positioning: Independent lectures that capture the authentic voice, teaching, and experience of Dr. Samuel Capelli. Each lecture stands alone as a written educational experience.
lectures.pullQuote: Knowledge is spoken in the moment. These lectures preserve that moment so it can continue to teach, long after the room is empty.

items.title: The Architecture of Human Choice
items.subtitle: Understanding the Mind Before the Action
items.synopsis: Human behavior does not begin with action. It begins with perception, thought, interpretation, and the emotional responses that influence our decisions. In this lecture, I examine the architecture of human choice and the processes that occur before behavior becomes visible. We explore how subconscious programming and emotional activation can influence our responses, often without conscious evaluation. The objective is to recognize the difference between reacting and choosing. When we develop awareness, examine the facts, and consider consequences before acting, we begin directing our lives with greater purpose. Choice is not simply the freedom to act. It is the responsibility to understand what we are choosing and why.
items.excerpt: When we talk about choice, most people believe they are choosing. But what is actually happening is a reaction based on perception, emotion, and conditioning. The first step is awareness. If you are not aware of what is happening inside you, then you are not choosing. You are reacting. And reaction is not freedom. Reaction is conditioning…
items.imageAlt: Lecture No. 001, The Architecture of Human Choice. Lectures in Print, Lecture No. 001, The Architecture of Human Choice. An armillary sphere and open book on a stone balustrade overlooking a river valley at sunrise.

items.title: Healthy Relationships
items.synopsis: Healthy relationships require more than affection, attraction, or the desire to remain together. They require individuals who understand communication, trust, responsibility, and respect. In this lecture, I examine the thinking and behavioral patterns that strengthen relationships and those that gradually create conflict, misunderstanding, and instability. We explore how personal perceptions, entitlement, emotional reactions, and the unwillingness to accept accountability can interfere with healthy communication. The objective is not to determine who is right or wrong, but to understand how our individual behavior contributes to the relationship. Before evaluating another person, we must first be willing to examine ourselves.
items.imageAlt: Lecture No. 002, Healthy Relationships. Cover art to come; the Lectures in Print emblem on navy.
items._artNote: COPY NEEDED: cover art for this lecture. Placeholder shows the Lectures in Print emblem until Sam sends the cover.

items.title: Emotional Regulation in Real Life
items.synopsis: Emotions are alarms. They communicate that something requires our attention, but they do not necessarily establish what is true or determine how we should respond. In this lecture, I examine the relationship among perception, subconscious programming, physiological activation, and behavioral choice. Through the Law of Order and the Law of Disorder, we explore how individuals can move from automatic reactions toward deliberate evaluation. Emotional regulation does not require us to eliminate anger, fear, frustration, or disappointment. It requires us to recognize the activation, investigate its meaning, examine the consequences, and determine an appropriate response. The objective is to learn how to experience emotion without surrendering responsibility for our behavior.
items.imageAlt: Lecture No. 003, Emotional Regulation in Real Life. A glowing brain illustration above a sunlit landscape.
items._artNote: Sam's cover art for this lecture still carries the interim number 002; his master catalog (Oct 26, 2026) makes it No. 003. Replace the art when he sends the renumbered cover.

items.title: The Thinking Model of Assessment™
items.synopsis: Thinking and evaluating are not necessarily the same process. Individuals can spend considerable time thinking while never questioning the accuracy of their assumptions or the consequences of their conclusions. In this lecture, I introduce the Thinking Model of Assessment™ as a structured approach to examining information, separating facts from interpretation, and evaluating decisions before they become actions. We explore the influence of emotion, perception, and previous experiences upon judgment. The objective is to develop disciplined thinking that does not simply defend what we already believe, but examines whether those beliefs are supported by the available information. Better decisions begin with better assessment.
items.imageAlt: Lecture No. 004, The Thinking Model of Assessment™. A stone stairway climbs toward mountains at dawn.
items._artNote: Sam's cover art for this lecture still carries the interim number 003; his master catalog (Oct 26, 2026) makes it No. 004. Replace the art when he sends the renumbered cover.

items.title: Responsibility Is a Life System
items.synopsis: Responsibility is not an occasional act of admitting a mistake. It is a continuous system through which we direct our thinking, behavior, relationships, and decisions. In this lecture, I examine responsibility as a principle of daily living, emphasizing the importance of accepting what belongs to us while recognizing what remains beyond our control. We explore the relationship among personal accountability, emotional regulation, behavioral consistency, and the consequences of our actions. The objective is to move beyond explanations and justifications toward meaningful application. We cannot continually demand different outcomes while repeating the same patterns. Responsibility begins when we become willing to examine our participation and make the necessary changes.
items.imageAlt: Lecture No. 005, Responsibility Is a Life System. A lone tree on a hillside at sunrise.
items._artNote: Sam's cover art for this lecture still carries the interim number 004; his master catalog (Oct 26, 2026) makes it No. 005. Replace the art when he sends the renumbered cover.

items.title: Trauma, Activation, and Choice
items.synopsis: Our past experiences can influence how we interpret present circumstances, particularly when those experiences involve fear, uncertainty, or psychological distress. In this lecture, I examine the relationship among trauma, subconscious activation, emotional regulation, and behavioral choice. We explore how previous experiences may influence perception and how the nervous system can respond to situations associated with earlier distress. The objective is not to dismiss the impact of trauma or suggest that every reaction is easily controlled. It is to understand the importance of awareness, therapeutic regulation, and the gradual development of purposeful responses. The past may influence our present, but understanding that influence creates opportunities for change.
items.imageAlt: Lecture No. 006, Trauma, Activation, and Choice. Balanced stones stacked beside still water at sunrise.
items._artNote: Sam's cover art for this lecture still carries the interim number 005; his master catalog (Oct 26, 2026) makes it No. 006. Replace the art when he sends the renumbered cover.

items.title: Relationships, Boundaries, and Personal Power
items.synopsis: Personal power begins with the ability to direct ourselves, not with the ability to control another individual. In this lecture, I examine the relationship among personal boundaries, emotional responsibility, communication, and respect for individual rights. We explore why healthy boundaries require clarity, consistency, and an understanding of what belongs to our responsibility. Boundaries are not instruments of punishment or domination. They establish how we choose to participate in relationships and what behaviors we are willing to accept. The objective is to develop relationships in which personal freedom and mutual respect can exist together. We must learn to direct our own lives without attempting to take ownership of someone else's.
items.imageAlt: Lecture No. 007, Relationships, Boundaries, and Personal Power. A stone arch bridge over a river gorge at sunrise.
items._artNote: Sam's cover art for this lecture still carries the interim number 006; his master catalog (Oct 26, 2026) makes it No. 007. Replace the art when he sends the renumbered cover.

items.title: The Capelli Respect Model™
items.synopsis: Respect begins with a fundamental principle: direct your life toward your own desires and dreams without violating the rights of others. In this lecture, I examine the meaning of that principle and the discipline required to put it into practice. We explore self-direction, behavioral control, emotional rights, disciplined thinking, and the importance of evaluating facts and consequences before acting. Respect is not simply politeness, agreement, or something we expect others to demonstrate. It is reflected in how we conduct ourselves, particularly when our desires conflict with another person's rights. The objective is not merely to understand the Respect Model, but to become the model through consistent application.

items.title: Healthy Relationships and Anchors
items.synopsis: A healthy relationship requires a foundation that can withstand disagreement, emotional activation, and the challenges of daily life. In this lecture, I examine four essential foundations: communication, trust, responsibility, and respect. We also explore the concept of anchors—patterns of thinking and behavior that prevent individuals and relationships from moving forward. These may include repeated mistakes, resistance to change, unresolved emotional patterns, and the unwillingness to accept accountability. The objective is to recognize how these anchors influence our decisions and what we must do to address them. Before asking whether someone else has become an anchor in our lives, we must examine whether we have become an anchor in our own.
